utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had indicated earlier the area where you were positioned on the 13th, near -- we've heard evidence in this trial before that this was a mass of people in the middle of the road. Do you see the area I'm indicating?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe to me-- or, in fact, mark on the aerial with a pen where this line that you're describing was.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understand it, the DutchBat soldiers spread out into, you said, a field. Can you indicate without marking, I suppose would be better, where this field that you're talking about is?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It's this meadow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the two houses that we see there on either side of your line.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me what you saw at that point -- first, excuse me, where were you on this line of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I was the last one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you witnessed at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but for the record, we need to make sure that when he's pointing, that they reflect where exactly or make some markings. Because later on, we will not be able to read from the transcript where the gentleman has pointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's a very good suggestion. Ms. Davis, you direct the witness to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can make an X on the approximate area where you were standing.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell us what you witnessed at that point.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: At a certain moment, my attention was attracted by a lot of shouting. A group of Serbian soldiers had taken a man along who was offering resistance. And I saw the men use a bit more aggression to take him along. They took him to the point I'm going to indicate now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can mark that as well.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: It has been marked with a dot, for the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what did you witness?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I saw the soldiers placing the man with his face to the wall, and from a distance of about 3 metres, shoot him through the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the first time you had seen the Muslim man?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No, just before that, my attention had already been attracted then as well by shouting, and it was the same person that was concerned. And I recognised him the second time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see him the first time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That was about here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how much time passed between when you saw him the first time and when you -- okay. I apologise. If you could mark the area that you just pointed to with an A, for the record.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How much time passed between when you first saw him being taken and when you saw the execution?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: About 10, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the man wearing?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Blue jeans, blue-green sweater.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for clarification, I'm speaking about the man who you saw being shot. Were they civilian clothes or military?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the man armed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Not as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the clothing of the BSA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It was Serbian camouflage in various shades, various colours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described that the man was shot in the head. Was it a single shot?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to the man after that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Immediately after he was hit by the bullet, he collapsed. And the four men who were nearby walked away a bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you estimate was the distance between where you were standing, marked with an X, and the spot that you marked with a dot on the aerial?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: About 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything obstructing your view?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No. At the utmost, the corner of the house as a result of which I couldn't see the face of the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the soldiers who were involved in this incident?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the area where this occurred was isolated or were there other people around?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Other people were walking around, but all of them were Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were other Serbian soldiers in the area?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice whether any of them had any reaction to what you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: They looked at the incident after hearing the shot, but then they continued their activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far would you estimate the shooting took place from the crowd of refugees?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: 100, 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your immediate reaction or your emotions when you saw the execution?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I got frightened at a certain stage and wanted to report it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you at some point have an opportunity to report what you saw?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Not that same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you report it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The next morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just have one final point of clarification, and then I'll be through. Do you remember giving a statement on September 29th, 1995, to a Dutch military policeman on behalf of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review that statement in the past few days?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- when you gave the statement, was there some confusion on your part about the dates on which these events have occurred?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, with hindsight, we found that I had shifted everything one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you certain about the dates that you have testified to today, that they're correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, I'm in your hands whether you are going to do your cross-examination or we have an early break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions, Your Honour, just one minor issue. So...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please, if you prefer to continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Corporal, first, thank you for coming. Second, I understand from the last question posed before coming here today, you had an opportunity to review the statement that you made back on I believe it was the 29th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I have another statement. It doesn't have a date to it, but it seems that you dictated and somebody was recording it as far as your observations, a two-page statement. Did you have an opportunity to read that? I received this from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understand it, back in I believe it was the 4th of July of 1996, you came before this Tribunal and you testified as well.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to review your transcript, it's fairly short?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So before coming here today, you had the benefit of reviewing what you had put down on -- as a statement and what you had testified orally in Court?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just have one question, and if you could help me out, I'd appreciate it: In none of these statements that I have before me, or the transcript from the testimony, do I see anywhere where you have indicated that certain refugees, folks over there in Potocari, who refused to get on the buses were first insulted, then were forced on to them. My question is, in reviewing your statements and in reviewing your transcript, were you able to find that, because I have not been able to?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Neither have I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the very first time that you're reporting this.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any cross-examination from Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we shall have several questions to ask this witness. In terms of time, I don't think it should take more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So what's your preference? We'll have our break now, or we'll finish your cross-examination, then have the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's up to the Court really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll have our early break. We'll resume at 20 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, your cross-examination, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Groenewegen. My name is Miodrag Stojanovic. I represent Mr. Dragan Jokic before this Tribunal. I would like to ask you a number of questions related to your testimony today and also related to what you said on the 4th of July, 1996, when you also testified before this Court. The way I understood your testimony today, you were at the checkpoint or rather observation post you referred to as Mike and November, the two observation posts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were there just before the tragic events in Srebrenica, that means until the 10th of July. Am I correct in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the interview you gave on the 4th of July, you said there was shooting from approximately observation posts Papa, shooting -- rather, fire at the aims or targets where you were stationed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Again, if we could have the witness shown his statement, if he's going to be referring to specific portions, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, do you have the statement at your hands? Is it possible to furnish it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have a statement here in B/C/S. But I have no intention of quoting the statement, so I will not be using the statement in such a way as to make it indispensable for the witness to actually have it before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed in this way. Let's see how extensive you're going to use that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This shooting, this fire, did you take that as a provocation since the actual targets were not being hit?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I, therefore, assume that you understood this firing or shooting by the other side as an attempt on their part to cut the road off towards Potocari for the population trying to get away?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I wrong in concluding that the objective of firing at your positions was also to keep the population in the same place that they were up to that point?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At one point you provided the following answer to the Prosecution. You said you had talked to one of them, having in mind members of the BH army, and they told you allegedly that it was better for them to fight than to head towards Potocari on a voluntary basis. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us exactly what you understood they meant by saying that.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It was clear that they knew what was going to happen if they went down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if they knew what would happen, what about the men, women, children, and disabled persons? Even if they knew what would happen, did they still have a reason in your view for going to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, it seems to me that your question is asking the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to rephrase my question, Your Honours. I do not want the witness to speculate. I want him to explain what exactly he meant when he said that he had been informed that it was better for them to fight rather than to go of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was, who were the people who headed off to Potocari of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They went of their own free will. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think they had no other option.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask another question along the same lines. During your testimony, you used the word "evacuation" on several occasions. This word, did you use it consciously? Do you distinguish between the concepts of evacuation and forcible relocation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I didn't choose that word consciously. I now know the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I, therefore, conclude that when you say "evacuation" you were speaking about everything that was going on with the refugees in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This evacuation, or whatever was going on in Potocari, was it the result of fear that you have referred to on several occasions today, fear that the population felt?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think there was any imperative military reason to have the population evacuated under war circumstances?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I wouldn't venture to say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take it that you are unable to actually answer this question? Is it that you don't know the reasons?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No, but I'm not an expert in this field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. At the beginning of today's testimony, you said that you observed the presence of the BH army in the enclave of Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "members of the BH army," what exactly do you mean? Which units and up to which level of units are we talking about in the context of what you saw?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Men with weapons willing to fight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of weapons?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Small-calibre weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also include in that definition small artillery weapons such as mortars?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I never observed them having that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about anti-armour, such as the Zolja or Osa grenade launchers?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Neither those. When we saw them, it was only small-calibre weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please tell us roughly, having in mind the area that you patrolled, what was the power, the actual force, of those units?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It could vary from groups of five up to ten men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they organised in a military way?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Not directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly does that mean, "not directly"? Did they have a command? Did they have a principle of military subordination and organisation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple more questions: You said in your interview that on that day, you had seen General Mladic. Is that correct, in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on the 12th or on the 13th, or both on the 12th and 13th?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Both days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did he stay there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: He's moving around constantly through the area taking along his regular military staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you draw the conclusion from his behaviour that he was actually in charge of the situation, that he was the man controlling the situation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His arrival on the 13th, was that prior to or after the killing of the young men that you talked about today?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Prior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I don't think I've understood the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prior to the murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he there when the killing took place?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after his departure did this happen?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: A couple of hours afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were standing about 30 metres from where this occurred, right, and also that you were scared, understandably?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope this is not a pretentious question. Why were you scared, or more specifically the reason for your fear then, was it fear of possible consequences for you and your personal safety?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you actually took any steps in order to stop the crime from happening in as far as it put you at risk?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It had happened before I had any time to think about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we believe the reason for your fear was precisely that.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm drawing the examination to a close. Just one more question: Does that also mean that anyone else in your shoes at that time trying to prevent it would have faced the same situation and the same things that you were up against?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another question, Your Honours, in view of the indictment against my client, as I am probably not likely to have occasion to re-examine this witness. Item 43 of the indictment talks about -- count 43 of the indictment talks about two crimes on the 12th of July in connection with opportunistic killings in Potocari. In the forest, next to the UN Compound on the Budak side of the main road, the bodies of nine men were found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another count, on the 12th of July, the same day, at about 700 metres from the UN base in the creek behind the white house, the bodies of nine or ten men were found. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours. Thank you, Witness. I apologise if you took any of my questions personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender into evidence? Yes, Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we just have two, and that would be P47 and P50. P20.1 on the list also was admitted previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if it has been admitted previously, you don't have to tender it once again. The effect is the same. Any objections? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those documents are admitted into evidence. As for the P50, was it admitted before or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: The same aerial was admitted in another form, Your Honour, but this exhibit was not. And it has now been marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Do you think we should have a different number on that piece of evidence? You mean, there are two documents. One is the original; the other is the document marked by the witness. So we'll have different numbers for those two --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: That would be fine with us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar will take care of this matter. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I don't have the indictment now and the numbers, and I think this is an opportunity, the excerpt from the video regarding the identification of the house, which the witness actually failed to identify any of the houses, for that matter, is it 50 or 51, exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think it's 48. Any objections from the Prosecution side?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: We don't have any objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This evidence is admitted as the evidence from the Defence side. The Madam Registrar will be instructed to give a Defence number on it. Thank you very much, Witness, for coming here to give your evidence. I wish you good luck in your future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for the next witness, are there any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You're pretty sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You are sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: May I ask permission to have Mr. Dragoslav Djukic leave the courtroom at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Or good evening, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Issa:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you state your name for the record, and spell your last name.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Leendert Cornelis Van Duijn. D-u-i-j-n.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand, sir, that you are a captain with the Dutch army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at present, sir, where are you serving?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At Schiphol airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that at one point you attended the royal military academy in Breda from 1989 to 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1993 you were commissioned into the army as a second lieutenant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the speakers slow down, please, for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1994, you were promoted as first lieutenant. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1995, you were deployed to Bosnia with DutchBat III as a platoon commander. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long, sir, had you spent with your platoon training prior to going out to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The training took about six months prior to deployment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, what was the average age of the men that were serving under you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Must have been around 19 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how old were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I was 24 at that time, turning 25 in May of that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the size of your platoon?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The size of my platoon was 34, if I'm not mistaken, 34 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were you subordinated to you? Who was your company commander?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: My company commander was Captain Matthijssen, in the Charlie company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you, sir, to think back to July 1995 and to specifically focus on the period between the 9th of July and 10th of July, and tell us where you were at that point?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At that point I was in the blocking position south of the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to us, sir, what is a blocking position?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: More or less literally the word says itself, we were supposed to take up a position south of the city with our APCs. And together with air supports, we should be able to stop the advancement of the Serb army that was advancing towards the city from the south to the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you try to stop the advancement of the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Because the Serb army was threatening the city itself, and shelling the city. And because it was a zone -- demilitarised zone where we should protect that area and the people that were in it, that was our focus, to prevent it from being taken by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. I'm just going to refer you to Prosecution Exhibit 20.1, which is a map. And I'm going to ask you, sir, if you could look at that map and indicate what your approximate position was at that time. Can you see it? Perhaps the usher can assist you. So what was your approximate position at that point?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: My approximate position was just south of the circle which says Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were, just for the record, you're indicating that you were south of the UN Bravo company. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And can you describe, sir, the scene on the 10th of July while you were in the blocking position?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We saw people, Muslim refugees, fleeing to the north, passing our position and trying to take everything they had with them as far as they could carry it. Some took food, some took blankets. The people were very scared, panicked, and they tried to get away from that location. We, on the other hand, took up our position there at that location south of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned earlier, sir, that there was shelling. Can you describe how long the shelling was going on.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The shelling was going on from even earlier than the 9th. It must have been started somewhere around the 6th. And at that time, when I was in the blocking position, it was constantly directed at our location or at the city itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, while you were in the blocking position, did you see the Muslim army at all?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I saw some Muslim soldiers, and they were actually at first glad that we were taking up a position there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And where did you see the Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Near to my location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: They were shooting in the direction of the south. It wasn't clear to me at what they were shooting, or they were shooting or they were moving towards the south or back again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, moving then to the 11th of July, 1995, can you tell us whether or not the refugees remained in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The refugees had by then all were vanished from my location. They were all going towards the compound of the Bravo company or more north to the compound of Charlie company, which was in Potocari. So practically all the refugees were fleeing to the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you leave the blocking position, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I left there in the afternoon when it was clear to us that not only the refugees, but also the Muslim soldiers had left there because at a later stage, they were scared that we would leave from that location and threatened to shoot at our APCs with an anti-tank rockets. So by the time that they had left, it was safer for us to leave as well. So that must have been around 12.00 or 1.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So can you describe to us, sir, the scene as you saw it when you left Srebrenica or the blocking position.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Srebrenica was empty. There was no one left. More or less sort of a ghost city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We went -- at first we went to the location of the UN Bravo company where a lot of refugees had packed together and were starting to move to the compound of Charlie company and the battalion headquarters in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you moved back to the compound in Srebrenica, did you see anybody on the road between Srebrenica and Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: No, that part of the city was totally abandoned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd just like to take you, sir, now to the evening of 11 July to 12 July. Can you tell us, sir, where you were that evening and what happened?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I was at a point we call point 02. That was south of the compound of the Charlie company in Potocari. It was the inner section that was the road to Susnjari and to the location of the OP or observation post Mike. We took up a position there with a few APCs because the APC of Sergeant Mulder that was stationed on OP Mike was coming back to the compound in Potocari, and there were a lot of refugees with him near his APC. So we took up a position to wait for him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know that Sergeant Mulder was coming back to that position?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He radioed in and said he was coming with a lot of refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So turning back to, sir, the map, Exhibit P20.1, can you indicate on the map where point 02 is, when you took that position?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Point 02 is the intersection from the road from Susnjari to Potocari, and where it crosses the road from Potocari on southwards to Srebrenica. So the intersection is called "point 02."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall the arrival of Sergeant Mulder that evening?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Our APCs were parked alongside the road. And his APC, he had parked it in the middle of our APCs. And it was packed with refugees. I spoke to Sergeant Mulder for about ten minutes, and in the meanwhile, my soldiers started to help the refugees to come off the APC. And the APC was totally covered with refugees, and alongside the APC was also sort of a caravan with a few hundred refugees that accompanied him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, around what time did he arrive in the evening?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That must have been around 11.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can then move on to 12 July, 1995, in the morning. Can you tell us where you were in the morning and what happened.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I was still near point 02, a little bit to the north. We had regrouped our APCs about a hundred metres to the north, hundred fifty metres maybe. And we heard that some Serb soldiers had been seen crossing near the compound of the Charlie company and the battalion headquarters in Potocari. And they were on the road. And we could see -- also see some soldiers crossing through the fields on the eastern side of the road, and coming on the road again at point 02, just south of our location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you heard that on the radio, sir, did you do anything, or what did you do?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We were ordered, Captain Groen from Bravo company was there as well, and we were ordered to assemble our small-calibre weapons, assemble them in one APC that was locked, and we got ordered to put our .50 calibre machine-gun on top of the APC, to point it to the sky to prevent possible escalation when the Serb troops came to our location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see, sir, what the Serbs were doing when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The Serbs that were coming to the fields from the eastern side of the road and getting on to the road at point 02, a few of the Serb soldiers kept standing on the road, a few Serbs entered houses and came out of the houses later on again. And it was my impression that they were checking if the houses were empty. And the other Serb soldiers that followed the road from north to south to our location, came to our location and started passing out of cigarettes and other stuff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did they pass out the cigarettes to?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: To the UN soldiers to, my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you describe the uniform of the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Green camouflage, but also combined with all sorts of shirts, bandannas, backpacks of all sorts of colours so more or less combined uniforms. One of the soldiers I remember had a Serb flag draped around his body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned, sir, that some of them had a backpack full of cigarettes which they passed out to your soldiers or the UN Dutch soldiers. What was your impression of that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: My impression of that was that they were trying very hard to show that they were nice guys, and they try to make friends of some sort with our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you also mentioned, sir, that some of them went into houses. Did you -- do you know who these houses belonged to?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I know that the Muslim refugees had been living in those houses for a few years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I understand that later on that morning, you met with Captain Groen. Is that right? Or company commander.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, he was still on my location there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know around what time this was?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At the end of the morning, maybe around 11.00 in the morning, 10.00, 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you discuss with him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: By then, it was more or less clear to us that we were no longer in control. We didn't have any control any more because basically our weapons were put away. So I was asking him what to do next, what would be happening next. And I wondered if I could do anything at all because we were more or less waiting there for events to take place. And Captain Groen said to me, we'll just go north, there's a big concentration of refugees just south of the UN base, and maybe you can help over there. And that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That was in Potocari, just south of the UN base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you -- you indicated you went there. And how many refugees did you see when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Scattered around the big factory sites, must have been around 20 or 30.000 refugees that were packed over there. It's very difficult to make an estimation, of course. But that's more or less my estimation, 20 to 30.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I went looking for the UN soldiers that were over there. And they were -- from the moment I came there looking at me as to ask what to do. And I heard about a stampede of refugees that were trying to get into the compound because they thought it was safer there. But I heard that the compound, our UN Compound, was already packed with refugees, so I got the order by radio not to lead anyone through again, to let anyone through towards the compound. So we organised UN soldiers, formed a human chain on the road, and try with the interpreter, tried to make it clear to the refugees that they could not go to the UN Compound and they had to stay there and try to find some shade, get out of the sun, and try to calm them down a little bit because they were very scared, panicked, more or less in shock from all the events that had taken place in the previous days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. I'm going to ask you, then, to refer to Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit P51, which is an aerial. If you see that on your screen, I'm going to ask you, sir, what position you took when you arrived, when you were directing the soldiers among the refugees.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It must have been in the middle of the road, in between the zinc factory, and the express bus compound, a little bit to the south on that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened next, sir? Do you recall meeting a member of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I remember that when we were trying to organise the UN soldiers, I remember that General Mladic came to that location, and there was a film crew with him, and he was trying to make sort of a propaganda movie handing out stuff to the refugees, talking to them. I could not understand what he was saying, but it was sort of a lightning visit by General Mladic at that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Prosecution Exhibit P56, I'm going to ask you if you -- I'm going to show you a photograph. And just for the record, you did have an opportunity to see these photographs when we met a few days ago. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I haven't got a picture --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did show you some photographs --

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: You did show me some photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also had an opportunity to watch portions of a video. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see anything on your screen right now, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I see a picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It has just come up on mine now. There was a bit of a delay. Can you identify the individuals in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I can see that the person on the left is General Mladic. And the person on the right is Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So let's just talk about Colonel Jankovic for a moment. Did you see him that day?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I had a conversation with him. He was standing there alone dressed in a camouflage uniform with a brown leather bag on his shoulder. And I was wondering what sort of a soldier he was. So I began a conversation with him, and he told me that he was a colonel, logistics officer, and he had fought in the war in 1991 and 1992, then went back to his business in Belgrade, and he was back for this part of the war again as a logistics officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you communicate with him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what did he appear to be doing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It looked to me like he was just looking around, more or less inspecting what was happening over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you indicated he mentioned to you that he was a logistics officer, and you had a brief conversation. Do you recall if he said anything else to you at that point?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was very strange because we were more or less just conversating about all sorts of things. And then he mentioned that I was more or less lucky because I was still alive. But he said it in a very strange fashion. And later, I have met Colonel Jankovic on several occasions, and he always -- we didn't have a long conversation the other times I spoke with him. He always pointed at me and just said, well, I see that you're still alive. That was the only thing he said to me, and he said it in a very strange way, so it made a big impression on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he always greeted you with that phrase.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall when was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The last time I saw him was when he was together with Colonel Karremans and Major Franken. And he was inspecting our compound. It was the day before we left. I think that was the 19th or the 20th of July, the day before we left to go to Zagreb. And we were told that there was a high-ranking Serb officer that was coming and inspecting what we would leave behind and what we would take with us. And I saw him walking together with Colonel Karremans and Major Franken. And he saw me as well, and he greeted me in the same way again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Getting back to the 12th of July, sir, can you tell us, what was the next significant thing that happened that you recall?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: After General Mladic went away, I met with a Serb captain whose name was Mane, and he had an interpreter with him called Miki. And he asked me if I was the local UN commander at that location, and I stated to him that I was. And he practically stated to me that the refugees were going away, that there were buses on the way, and they would be there in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll get back to that conversation in a moment. Do you know, sir, what military unit that Captain Mane belonged to?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He said he was from a military police unit, and he had a sort of liaison with the Drina Corps or Drina Wolves. As I understood, the Drina Corps and the Drina Wolves were the same unit. And he had a sort of liaison -- he was not part of the Drina Corps, but he had a liaison with that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to Prosecution Exhibit 52, which is another photograph that I'd like you to take a look at, do you see that on your screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I see, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you recognise any individuals on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The person on the left is the Serb captain named Mane, and the person on the right is myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just another photograph, Prosecution Exhibit 53. Can you tell us if you recognise that individual.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That person is Mane as well, the Captain Mane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your conversation with him, sir, did you have occasion to learn who Captain Mane's commander was?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He said that his commander had -- I only know the commander by his nickname, the code name used on the radio, and that code name was Stalin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the only name that you knew him by?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, only by his nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you seen Stalin before?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I hadn't seen him before, but I saw him later that day. And Mane pointed him out to me and said that that was his commander, code name Stalin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you get a general description from Mane as to what Stalin looked like?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The general description he gave was he was a short fellow with a big moustache and big Ray Ban glasses on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. If I can then refer you to Prosecution Exhibit P54 and ask you if you recognise anybody on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Person on the right is the person I know as Stalin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And turning then to Prosecution Exhibit P55, do you recognise anybody in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The person on the left, I know as Stalin, and the person in the middle is General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Getting then back to the conversation you had with Mane, can you tell us what else did he tell you? What else did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Well, he practically told me that the refugees were going to leave, that there was no discussion about. He only said to me, well, you have the choice of staying here or leaving. And then we'll do it our own way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he mean by that? What did you understand that to mean "we'll do it our own way"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will object on the basis of speculation. She is asking the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: My submission, Your Honour, it's not speculation. He was having a conversation with Mane, and he may be able to explain why he understood what he understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may ask some questions about the conversations around this sentence so that we could understand the circumstances in which the sentence he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything else to you, sir, aside from "you can either leave or we can do it our own way"?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That was more or less the phrase that he used. And he said that the buses were on their way. And I got the impression from the way he said it that it was better for us to stay there and practically stand in between the Serbs and the Muslim refugees to try and prevent that anything bad would happen to the refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So when you say it was better for you to stay there and stand in between the Muslims -- the Muslim refugees and the Serbs, to prevent anything bad from happening to them, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Well, you can see that the situation that we were practically in a few days shelled from the southern part of the city to the location that we were there, that there was a lot of violence used in the war before, which I knew from the scenes I had seen on television. It was better for us, and I thought it was a role from the UN soldiers, that they would be in between so that the refugees were not being handled in any bad way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what was the condition of the refugees at that time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: They were very scared, of course. Tired. It was 35 degrees centigrade. It was very warm. They were practically in a state of shock from the situation from the few days before. And they were particularly very scared and more or less panicky.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Did you at some point find out who Stalin was subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I remember a visit from Stalin with a man I knew as Major Nikolic. And from the way they came to our location, it was my idea that Nikolic was the commander of Stalin; Stalin was more or less explaining what was happening on that location, and he was speaking to him in a way, and Major Nikolic was walking and looking around in a way that I got the impression that Major Nikolic was the commander of the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later that day, sir, I understand that you saw General Mladic for a second time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That must have been about, in the afternoon, about 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to us, sir, what he was doing the second time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He came up to me and wanted to speak to me, wanted to speak to the commander of the UN unit there. And that was me, of course. And he spoke with me and a few of my soldiers and my interpreter. My Muslim interpreter was there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: First the conversation was more or less about all sorts of things, about sports, about soccer, all sorts of things that came up about sports. Then he asked me a question about one of the soldiers that was there as well. And he was a soldier, a black soldier, Dutch soldier. And he said to me that he was more or less surprised that -- and wondering if that was a Dutch soldier or not. And I explained to him that we have a multiracial society in Holland. That was as well a Dutch soldier. And then he stated to me that that was not good, that we had a multiracial society, and that the Muslims would be -- sorry, the Serbs would be in Holland in ten years from that day to help the Dutch against the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do anything else, sir, or say anything else?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He made a sort of role play with my Muslim interpreter who had been in a tricky situation because his UN pass was taken away by the bodyguards of Mladic. And he asked me, he put his arm around the Muslim interpreter, and he asked me what nationality that interpreter had. And I answered him that he was Muslim. And then he continued in a sort of role play, and General Mladic said, well no you're wrong. This is Serb, and he pointed at my Muslim interpreter, this is a Serb, this is a good guy. And I, and he pointed himself, I'm a Muslim, I'm a bad guy, bad person, and I'm only interested about making babies and he crushed the Muslim interpreter to his body, and it was obvious to me that the Muslim interpreter was very scared. It was a sort of bizarre role play that General Mladic was playing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, sir, that the UN pass for the Muslim interpreter was taken. Can you tell us by whom?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: By the bodyguards that accompanied General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We later on, we managed to get the pass back from the bodyguards for Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did General Mladic stay at your position?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He stayed there for about half an hour, 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was your conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I think that took about 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While General Mladic was present, was the transportation process ongoing?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The process was ongoing, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular incident while General Mladic was present involving the transportation process of the refugees out of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I remember that after the conversation, General Mladic went a little bit north from our location, about 50 metres, and he was standing there with his interpreter. And I remember that a Muslim woman was very panicked, she was screaming. And one of my soldiers got her out of the crowd, and through my interpreter, we asked what was going on. And she said that her five children she had lost in the crowd were already put on one of the trucks, and it was the last truck from the caravan. And we could see the children in the back of the truck waving towards us and their mother. And I decided then to bring the mother to the truck, and was about maybe, a hundred, hundred fifty metres from our location. And General Mladic was in the middle of the distance. And I asked my interpreter to help me, to go up to General Mladic because we had a sort of an understanding that you had the Muslim refugees, we were standing in the middle of the Muslim refugees and the Serb soldiers. So behind our location, there was -- the area was only -- the only people that were in that area were the Serb soldiers near to the buses. So I was more or less crossing the border where we normally would not be, UN soldiers, I mean. So I asked the Muslim interpreter to help me to go up to General Mladic because he was the ranking officer there and explain what I was doing because I was crossing that border. And I carried the woman to the truck, put her in the back of the truck. And when I returned, I saw the Muslim interpreter standing near to General Mladic, and I was glad that he helped me, that he explained to General Mladic what was going on because I was afraid that any of the Serb soldiers would think that was a strange action and maybe shoot at me or do something else. And the only thing -- the only person I knew that could prevent that was General Mladic. And when I came to General Mladic, he said that I was a little bit crazy to do such a thing, but he was terribly angry about not what I had done, but about the fact that the Muslim interpreter had come to him and started speaking without it being obvious that he was interpreting for me. So General Mladic was very angry with me and the Muslim interpreter, and he said if that would happen again, he would shoot the interpreter there single-handedly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just clarify why he said he would shoot the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Because the interpreter was speaking to him directly, not in a way that he was interpreting for me and saying the things to General Mladic what I was saying, but because he was directly speaking to General Mladic, General Mladic was very angry with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you recall, sir, what was happening in Potocari next, after that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The transports continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you describe the transportation process.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Transportation process was more or less the buses arrived, Captain Mane would tell me how many buses there were and to prevent the buses and the trucks being packed with refugees, we would let a number of people through in a way that they wouldn't trample each other or push each other to the ground. And in small groups, that they would be able to enter the buses and the trucks in a quiet, calm way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, did you observe how the Muslims were being treated by the Bosnian Serb soldiers while they were boarding the buses?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I heard that while they were boarding the buses, some of our soldiers were there. They saw that they were kicked and pushed into the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, what was the composition of the groups of people who boarded the buses.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Mainly women and children, and there were not that many men there in the big group of refugees. But after a while, when the transports were ongoing, I noticed that the men were singled out from the rest of the group that was going towards the buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see how the men were singled out?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: A few incidents I remember because it happened on the location where we were. But most of the time, it happened behind our location and was more or less that they were speaking in Serbo-Croat, so I couldn't understand. And practically were told that they should leave the rest of the group and go and sit on a lawn in front of a few houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you do when you saw the men being singled out?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I confronted the Serb captain Mane with what I saw. And he explained to me that they wanted to see if the men from Srebrenica were war criminals or not. And that they had a list in Bratunac where they would compare the names with the names of the men, and they would see if they were war criminals or not. And if they were war criminals, they would be kept as prisoners of war. And if they were not, they would be grouped back with the rest of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after receiving this explanation from Captain Mane, what did you do when you saw specific men being singled out?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Because his explanation was that they were looking for soldiers or war criminals, as he stated it, when there was a very young boy or a very old man singled out, I protested and said to him, well, you can't be serious, that cannot be a soldier or couldn't be a soldier. And he would let them go with their families again. So we protested in every way that we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to protest in relation to all the men?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Because men that were dressed in camouflage trousers or shirts, they really looked fit, 20, 30 years of age, that would possibly had been a soldier in the war, then it would be -- it would have lost its effect if I had protested with every man that was singled out. And of course, you have the people that are in the grey area that you think, well, should I protest or not? But when the men looked really -- looked like soldiers or could have been soldiers, then I didn't protest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe, sir, the clothing of the majority of the men that were singled out? What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to just refer you to the last Prosecution exhibit before we end for the day, referring to Prosecutor's Exhibit 51, which is the aerial that we referred to earlier. You see that on your screen?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I see it now, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, sir, that the men that were being separated out on this day were taken to a lawn in front of a house. Can you tell us approximately where is that located.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The houses were more or less adjacent to the zinc factory, so more or less in between the zinc factory and the white house, because they weren't kept in the white house. That was only on the second day. But there must be two houses in the middle. I can't see that very well on this screen. But it was on the right side of the road, on the western side of the road, and in between the white house and the zinc factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all right. This is as you say a different house than the white house than we've heard of earlier.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe to us, sir, what was the condition of this house?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The houses had a small lawn in front of them. The houses had no windows, very damaged houses, two houses next to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And were they taken to both these houses next to each other or to one?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: On the lawn in front of the two houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long, sir, did the men stay on the lawn outside these two houses?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The rest of the day until it was getting dark. I think about 8.00, half past 8.00 in the evening. Then they were -- they were picked up by a lorry I recognised from earlier that day because it also was there when bringing bread. And with that lorry, they were transported out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time, sir, did the transportation of the Muslim refugees stop that day?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That must have been around -- a little bit before the men were taken away, so that must have been around half past 7.00, 8.00 or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And can you tell us, sir, what direction were the men taken away to?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: To the north, to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, this might actually be a good time to end for the day. I do have other areas that I'm going to be getting into, subject, of course, Your Honour. Perhaps it might be a good time. It's 5 minutes to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll stop here and you'll continue tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, I have to warn you that you are still under the oath. So during your testimony, do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about the contents of your testimony. We'll see you tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The proceeding is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
